title: 10,000-dollar step tax-cost model with character comparison
scope: Illustrative federal and California income-tax amounts for a California resident who files single or married filing separately, with the selected amount treated as total taxable income, shown under each candidate tax character of Kalshi event-contract profit so the differences can be compared at every step.

model.filing_status: Single for federal purposes; Schedule X (single or married/RDP filing separately) for California
model.character: The open question is what kind of income the contract profit is. Instead of deciding it, the model computes the same amount under each candidate character. Ordinary, short-term capital, and wagering share the federal ordinary rate table; section 1256 (60/40) and long-term capital use the section 1(h) stacking rule with the 2026 breakpoints. California uses Schedule X for every scenario because FTB says California has no lower capital-gain rate.
model.amount_definition: The selected amount is modeled as taxable income, not gross deposits, contract notional, account balance, or a Kalshi statement total.
excludes: wagering-loss and capital-loss calculations (loss rules are described, not computed)
year-end mark-to-market timing differences under section 1256
the California Tax Table rounding used at or below $100,000 (F49)
model.california_note: The California side uses the official 2025 Schedule X rate schedule. The current research record does not contain a final 2026 California individual rate schedule; the 2026 FTB estimated-tax instructions direct filers to use the 2025 tax table for that worksheet. Do not relabel the 2025 schedule as a 2026 final return calculation.
model.stacking_rule: Section 1(h)(1): compute ordinary tax on taxable income minus the net capital gain; then 0 percent on the capital gain that fits below the maximum zero rate amount, 15 percent on the remainder up to the maximum 15-percent rate amount, 20 percent above that. Section 1(j)(5) supplies the dollar breakpoints.

scenarios.label: Ordinary income
scenarios.federal_note: Whole amount taxed on the 2026 ordinary rate table.
scenarios.california_note: Schedule X on the whole amount.
scenarios.loss_rule: Not the $3,000 capital-loss cap and not the wagering cap. No IRS page retrieved assigns this path to event contracts.
scenarios.forms: Schedule 1 (Form 1040) if reported as other income. Not confirmed by an IRS page for these contracts.
scenarios.evidence: Section 61 includes the profit (F01). No IRS page assigns any character (F03, F50).

scenarios.label: Short-term capital gain (held one year or less)
scenarios.federal_note: Net short-term capital gain is taxed as ordinary income at graduated rates, so the federal dollars match the ordinary row.
scenarios.california_note: Schedule X on the whole amount. No lower California rate.
scenarios.loss_rule: Losses net against capital gains; excess deductible against other income up to $3,000 ($1,500 married filing separately), with carryforward.
scenarios.forms: Form 8949 and Schedule D, if this character is used.
scenarios.evidence: Topic 409 (F04, F05, F08, F09). Whether an event contract is a capital asset under section 1221 has not been line-read.

scenarios.label: Section 1256 contract (60% long-term / 40% short-term)
scenarios.federal_note: 40 percent taxed first on the ordinary table; 60 percent stacked on top at 0/15/20 percent using the 2026 breakpoints (section 1(h), section 1(j)(5)).
scenarios.california_note: Schedule X on the whole amount. FTB: no lower rate for capital gains. Whether California marks open contracts to market at year-end is open (F42).
scenarios.loss_rule: Capital-loss rules apply to the 60/40 split; open positions are marked to market on the last business day of the year.
scenarios.forms: Form 6781 is the form titled for section 1256 contracts. Its instructions were not line-read, so line numbers are not stated.
scenarios.evidence: Requires the contract to be a section 1256 contract. The primary record weighs against a casual claim: Kalshi Klear calls the contracts fully collateralized swaps that are not traded on margin (F21, F43); section 1256(b)(2)(B) excludes swaps and similar agreements (F18); section 1256(g)(1) requires a mark-to-market deposit system (F45); and 60/40 never applies to gain that is otherwise ordinary (F46).

scenarios.label: Long-term capital gain (held more than one year)
scenarios.federal_note: Whole amount treated as adjusted net capital gain: 0 percent up to $49,450, 15 percent up to $545,500, 20 percent above (2026, single). This is the lowest federal bound in the model.
scenarios.california_note: Schedule X on the whole amount. Holding period does not lower the California rate.
scenarios.loss_rule: Same capital-loss rules as the short-term row.
scenarios.forms: Form 8949 and Schedule D, if this character is used.
scenarios.evidence: Only for a capital asset actually held more than one year, counted from the day after acquisition (F04). Most event contracts resolve inside a year, so this row is a bound, not an expectation.

scenarios.label: Wagering (gambling) income
scenarios.federal_note: Winnings are reported on Schedule 1 and taxed at ordinary rates, so the federal dollars match the ordinary row when the amount is already net taxable income.
scenarios.california_note: Schedule X on the whole amount.
scenarios.loss_rule: Federal: losses deductible only if itemizing, only to the extent of gains, and only 90 percent of losses for tax years beginning after 31 December 2025. California does not conform to the 90 percent limitation. The real burden can therefore exceed this row when there are losses.
scenarios.forms: Schedule 1 for winnings; Schedule A for losses (federal).
scenarios.evidence: Topic 419 (F26, F27), section 165(d) (F28), FTB nonconformity (F29). Sports-outcome contracts are the closest analogy; no IRS page names event contracts.
